analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional map-drawing away from politicians and gives it to independent state commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress after being referred there on its introduction day.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the practice of letting state legislators draw the boundaries of their own congressional districts. Every state would have had to use an independent commission, with limits designed to keep politicians' own seats safe out of the equation. It also would have banned mid-decade redistricting — the practice of redrawing maps again between censuses to squeeze out more seats. It died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states where congressional maps are drawn to protect incumbents and one party. Independent commissions with strict criteria — no considering an incumbent's home address, no considering party affiliation — tend to produce districts that follow communities rather than political advantage, and the ban on repeat redistricting would stop legislatures from rewriting maps mid-decade when a single election outcome displeased them. The public would also get an open process: public meetings, a public website, and the right to submit their own map proposals.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to draw congressional districts through an independent commission rather than the state legislature [S2][S3].
Bars a state from redistricting more than once after each census unless a court orders it, which would block mid-decade map redraws for partisan gain [S2][S3].
Prohibits the commission from considering an incumbent's residence or voters' party affiliation, the two ingredients of a gerrymander [S3].
Mandates open public meetings, a public website with mapping data and interactive software, and public input sessions across the state [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative leaders, who would lose the power to draw the district lines that determine who can defeat them and how safe their seats are. State parties would also lose their role in carving districts. Taxpayers would fund federal payments to states — $150,000 per representative per state — to run the commissions, and if a state failed to set up a commission, a federal court would draw its map instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent lawmakers and state party leaders

drawbacks.text: The commission is not fully independent of politicians: its members are appointed by the majority and minority leaders of each chamber of the state legislature [S3].

If a commission's plan is not enacted, or a state never forms one, the state's highest court or a federal district court selects or draws the map — putting unelected judges in charge of district boundaries [S2][S3].
The bill is a federal mandate overriding state control of redistricting, a constitutional arrangement some states have long defended [S3].
The federal payments — $150,000 per House seat, funded by appropriations — are a new recurring cost every ten years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: ordinary voters get districts drawn without regard to incumbents' safety, at the cost of some federal money, a weaker form of 'independent' than the name suggests, and court-drawn maps as the fallback. The commission design still routes appointments through legislative leaders of both parties, so it softens but does not eliminate politicians' influence. On balance it is a genuine anti-gerrymandering reform, though not the strongest version of one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, then to a subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Cooper introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties [S5].
One Democratic colleague cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].
No further action was ever taken on the bill, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative leaders kept the power to draw their own district lines for another decade, and the map-drawing parties keep the ability to protect safe seats.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent lawmakers who draw their own maps

for.name: Rep. Jim Cooper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 116th Congress

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire Congress without scheduling a hearing or markup after its day-one referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew a single Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support, and since it never reached the floor there was no recorded vote to show how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative leaders
industries.note: The bill would strip them of the power to draw the congressional map, including the prohibition on considering where incumbents live. Keeping that power lets officeholders shape the electorate; its preservation runs against voters' interest in fair districts.

The bill removes party leaders from direct control of map-drawing and requires equal appointees from each major party on the commissions. Parties lose a tool for maximizing seats and protecting safe districts.
